title: Question 1
stem:
A well has a depth of $36\text{ m}$ from ground level to the surface of the water in the well, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

{{figure:figure_1_1}}

Fig. 1.1 (not to scale)

A student wishes to find the depth of the well. The student plans to drop a stone down the well and record the time taken from releasing the stone to hearing the splash made by the stone as it enters the water.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Assume that air resistance is negligible and that the stone is released from rest.

Calculate the time taken for the stone to fall from ground level to the surface of the water.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the motion after the stone leaves the hand - what is its speed at the instant of release and what makes it speed up all the way down?

Hint 2: You know distance $s = 36\text{ m}$, starting speed and acceleration $g$. Recall how $s$, $u$, $a$ and $t$ are linked when starting from rest, rearrange for $t$ first, then put the numbers in.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise free fall from rest**
You are told air resistance is negligible and the stone is released from rest. That means initial velocity $u = 0$ and the only acceleration is due to gravity, $a = g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards. Distance fallen is $s = 36\text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Pick the equation with no final velocity**
For constant acceleration: $$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$$ With $u = 0$ this simplifies to: $$s = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$$ Rearranging for time: $$t = \sqrt{\frac{2s}{g}}$$

Step 3: **Substitute and calculate**
$$t = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 36}{9.81}} = \sqrt{7.34} \approx 2.71\text{ s}$$ To 2 significant figures, $t = 2.7\text{ s}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The time recorded by the student using a stop-watch is not equal to the time in **(a)**.

Suggest **three** possible reasons, other than the effect of air resistance, for this difference.

markscheme_points.text: reaction time between hearing the splash and stopping the stop-watch
the sound (of the splash) takes time to reach the student or the sound being heard or the sound (of the splash) has to travel to the student
the student might not let go of the stone from ground level
the student might not let go of the stone and start the stop-watch at the same time
stop-watch may not be properly calibrated / has a zero error
stone given initial velocity / initial velocity not zero
stone does not fall (exactly) vertically / in a straight line

hints: Hint 1: Think about what the stop-watch really records - it runs from release until the splash is heard at the top. Is that exactly the fall time?
Hint 2: Think about the person operating the watch - can you press start and stop at exactly the right instants?
Hint 3: Think about the release itself and the numbers you assume - was the stone truly dropped from rest exactly at ground level with $g$ exactly $9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$?
parts.proper_answer: Any three, e.g.: reaction time delay between hearing splash and stopping watch; time taken for sound of splash to travel 36 m up to student; stone not released from rest / given downward push; release and starting watch not simultaneous; stone not released from ground level.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Extra time for sound to travel up**
The time in (a) is only the downward fall of the stone. The student stops the watch when the sound is heard. Sound needs about $36/340 \approx 0.1\text{ s}$ to travel up the well, so the measured time is longer.

Step 2: **Human reaction and synchronisation**
A person cannot start the watch at exactly the instant of release and cannot stop it at exactly the instant of hearing. There is a reaction time delay, especially in stopping after hearing the splash. Starting late or stopping late shifts the reading.

Step 3: **Release conditions are not ideal**
If the stone is thrown down rather than just released, $u > 0$ and the fall is quicker. If it is released below or above ground level, $s$ is not 36 m. If it hits the side and does not fall vertically, the path is longer. Also local $g$ may not be exactly $9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and the watch may have zero error.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The student repeats the experiment three times and uses the results to calculate the depth of the well. The values are shown in Table 1.1.

Table 1.1

|  | 1st experiment | 2nd experiment | 3rd experiment |
| depth/m | 54.4 | 53.9 | 54.1 |

The true depth of the well is $36.0\text{ m}$. Explain why these results may be described as precise but not accurate.

markscheme_points.text: precise: results are close together / have little scatter
not accurate: the values are not close to / 50% different / (very) different from true value

hints: Hint 1: Look at the spread of the three values 54.4, 53.9 and 54.1 m - how close are they to each other and what word describes small scatter?
Hint 2: Now compare those values, around 54 m, with the true value of 36.0 m - how close are they to the truth and what word describes that?
parts.proper_answer: Precise because the three values are very close together with little scatter (range only 0.5 m). Not accurate because ~54 m is very different from / much larger than the true value of 36.0 m.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Check precision - agreement between repeats**
Precision means how close repeated readings are to each other, showing good repeatability. Here $54.4$, $53.9$ and $54.1\text{ m}$ all lie within $0.5\text{ m}$, so scatter is very small. The results are precise.

Step 2: **Check accuracy - agreement with true value**
Accuracy means how close the result is to the true value. The average is about $54\text{ m}$, which is about 50% larger than the true $36.0\text{ m}$. The results are far from the truth, so they are not accurate. This pattern suggests a systematic error, such as including sound travel time and reaction time every time.

key_concepts: precision as repeatability and small scatter
accuracy as closeness to true value
